title: Rest, life, and a home with God
overview: Genesis 2 moves from God’s rest into the garden, the human calling, and the first marriage. Read with Yeshua in view, the chapter opens into the Bible’s hope of life restored, people brought near to God, and creation made whole.

1.context: The heavens, earth, and all their host are brought to completion.
1.connection: John takes us back to this beginning and names the Word through whom all things came to be. Colossians says all things were created through Yeshua and hold together in him. The finished world in this verse belongs to the work of the living Messiah.

2.context: God ceases from His work on the seventh day.
2.connection: The writer of Hebrews reaches back to God’s seventh-day rest and invites people to enter God’s rest by trusting Him. Yeshua also calls the weary to come to him and find rest. The day’s quiet points toward the rest God gives, and Yeshua welcomes people into it.

3.context: God blesses the seventh day and sets it apart because He rested from His work.
3.connection: Yeshua says the Sabbath was made for people, and he names himself Lord of the Sabbath. That brings the seventh day’s blessing into focus: God’s holy time is a gift for life, and Yeshua teaches with authority about its purpose.

4.context: This verse marks the account of the heavens and earth and names the LORD God as their Maker.
4.connection: John opens his Gospel with the same words, “In the beginning,” then tells us the Word was with God and all things came through him. John identifies that Word with Yeshua. Genesis names the Maker; John brings the Messiah into that creation witness.

5.context: The field has not grown, rain has not fallen, and no human has come to work the ground.
5.connection: Genesis is about to introduce the first man’s calling. Paul later sets Adam beside Yeshua: the first Adam receives life, while the last Adam becomes the source of life. That contrast helps us see the human story beginning here and the life Yeshua brings to its rescue.

6.context: Water rises from the earth and waters the soil.
6.connection: Water makes the ground ready for life here. Yeshua later speaks of water he gives that becomes a spring of life within a person. The scene is not the same event, but the Bible carries water forward as a picture of the life God gives through Yeshua.

7.context: God forms the man from the dust and breathes life into him.
7.connection: Paul calls Adam the first man and Yeshua the last Adam. Adam’s story brings death into view; Yeshua, risen from the dead, gives life. The same God who breathed life into the first man has raised the Messiah and promises life through him.

8.context: God plants a garden in Eden and places the man there.
8.connection: The Bible’s story ends with God dwelling with His people and the tree of life standing in the renewed creation. Revelation’s garden-like picture answers the loss that begins later in Eden. Yeshua promises the one who overcomes a place at the tree of life.

9.context: The garden’s trees are beautiful and good for food; the tree of life and the tree of knowing good and evil are named.
9.connection: The tree of life does not disappear from Scripture. Revelation shows it beside the river of life in God’s renewed world, with its leaves bringing healing. Yeshua says he is the resurrection and the life; in him, the Bible’s hope of life reaches its heart.

10.context: A river waters Eden and divides into four branches.
10.connection: Eden’s river flows outward to water the garden. Revelation gives us a final vision of the river of life flowing from God’s throne and the Lamb, with the tree of life beside it. The picture carries the hope of God’s life reaching His whole creation through the Lamb.

11.context: Pishon circles Havilah, a land where the account says gold is found.
11.connection: Genesis remembers the land’s gold as a sign of its real abundance. Revelation later pictures God’s holy city with streets of pure gold. That echo is a glimpse of creation’s beauty brought into God’s promised future, where the Lamb is its light.

12.context: Havilah is described by its gold, bdellium, and onyx.
12.connection: The precious materials named here return in the Bible’s picture of the holy city—gold and stones set into its foundations. Revelation ties that splendor to God dwelling with His people and to the Lamb. What Genesis describes as earth’s treasure becomes part of the hope of a world made new.

13.context: The second river, Gihon, is linked with the land of Cush.
13.connection: The name Cush reaches beyond this one river description into the story of the nations. The prophets speak of people coming from far away to worship God, and the good news reaches an Ethiopian official in Acts. Yeshua’s message goes out across borders and brings people near to Israel’s God.

14.context: The Tigris and Euphrates complete the river list, with the Tigris placed east of Assyria.
14.connection: These river names place the story in the world around Israel. Isaiah looks ahead to the root of Jesse—the Messiah—who gathers the scattered people of God from the ends of the earth. The geography here becomes part of the larger biblical story of scattering and gathering.

15.context: God puts the man in Eden to cultivate the garden and guard it.
15.connection: The garden is entrusted to the man as a place to serve and protect. Yeshua calls himself the good shepherd, who lays down his life for the sheep. His faithful care shows the heart of authority: not grasping, but serving and guarding the life entrusted to you.

16.context: God gives the man permission to eat from every tree in the garden.
16.connection: The command begins with abundance. Yeshua points people to the Father’s care for food and daily needs, and he calls himself the bread of life. Together those words bring us back to the generous God who gives life and sustenance.

17.context: God forbids eating from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil and warns the man about death.
17.connection: Paul traces sin and death through Adam, then proclaims life through Yeshua. The warning in Eden is not the end of the story: through the Messiah’s obedience, God’s gift of life answers the reign of death.

18.context: God says it is not good for the man to be alone and promises a matching helper.
18.connection: God’s answer to the man’s loneliness is a relationship of shared life. Yeshua later teaches about marriage by returning to the creation account, and Paul speaks of marriage as a picture of Messiah’s faithful love for his people. This verse begins that story of covenant love and companionship.

19.context: God brings the animals and birds to the man, who names them.
19.connection: The naming shows the human calling to care for creation, yet the man still has no partner who shares his nature. Hebrews quotes the creation song about humanity’s place over God’s works, then turns our eyes to Yeshua, crowned with glory and honor. He carries the human calling toward its true purpose.

20.context: The man names the animals, but none is a fitting human counterpart.
20.connection: The animals cannot share the man’s human life; God has made people for relationship with one another. Hebrews says Yeshua shared flesh and blood with his family and became like them. In him, God comes near to humanity and brings people into one family.

21.context: God puts the man into deep sleep and takes from his side.
21.connection: The man’s deep sleep comes before the woman is brought to him, and God is the one who acts. Paul later reaches back to this marriage story when he speaks of Messiah’s self-giving love for his people. The shared life of the first couple helps Paul describe a faithful, protecting love.

22.context: God forms the woman from the man’s side and brings her to him.
22.connection: God brings the woman to the man as a gift of shared life and companionship. Paul quotes this marriage story while describing Messiah’s care for his people—nourishing them and holding them close. The connection is the faithfulness and unity of a joined relationship.

23.context: The man calls the woman bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh.
23.connection: The man recognizes kinship: she shares his very flesh and bone. Hebrews says Yeshua likewise shared flesh and blood with his brothers and sisters; John says the Word became flesh. The Messiah comes near to us by sharing real human life.

24.context: A man leaves his parents, holds fast to his wife, and the two become one flesh.
24.connection: Yeshua quotes this very verse when he teaches about marriage. Paul then says the one-flesh union points to Messiah and his people. Here the connection is direct: Yeshua himself brings Genesis’s words into his teaching, and the apostles unfold their picture of faithful unity.

25.context: The man and his wife are naked together and feel no shame.
25.connection: This first picture of life together is open and unafraid. The Bible’s final hope is that God will dwell with His people, wipe away every tear, and remove death and pain. Through Yeshua, the Lamb, that restored closeness with God is promised to the world.
